system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2156-10-16 22:14:00 to 2156-10-22 18:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a two-week history of abdominal distention, nausea, poor appetite, and constipation, with a single episode of vomiting on the day of admission. She has a complex medical history including chronic graft-versus-host disease, gastroparesis, and chronic opiate use for back pain. Abdominal X-ray revealed fecal loading, supporting constipation as a primary contributor to her symptoms. She was treated with an enema and bowel prep, which resolved her nausea and improved her abdominal discomfort. She underwent an EGD and colonoscopy, which revealed gastric nodules and a colonic ulcer with inflammation; biopsies were taken to evaluate for medication effects, infection, or GVHD. Dicyclomine was discontinued, metoclopramide was increased, and she was discharged on daily Miralax to prevent recurrence. She tolerated oral intake, remained stable, and was discharged home in improved condition with plans to follow up on biopsy results and with her GI specialist.
problems: Other specified disorders of stomach and duodenum
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  MR ___

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with CML s/p SCT with GVHD, CVID on IVIG,
presents with ongoing abd pain, diarrhea, and colonic bx with colitis unclear
etiology // evaluate small intestine for presence of inflammation or infection

TECHNIQUE:  T1 and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen and pelvis
were acquired within a 1.5 T magnet, including 3D dynamic sequences performed
prior to, during, and following the administration of 0.1 mmol/kg of Gadavist
intravenous contrast (7 cc). Oral contrast consisted of 900 mL of VoLumen. 1.0
mg of Glucagon was administered IM to reduce bowel peristalsis.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior imaging, the last are CT from ___ and MRCP
from ___.

FINDINGS: 

MR ENTEROGRAPHY:

The caliber and appearance of the small bowel is normal.  There are no
abnormally dilated or strictured segments.  The small bowel wall has normal
thickness and enhancement.  Bowel motility is normal.
Diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon is present.  Mild mucosal hyper
enhancement in the nondistended sigmoid colon (1101:57) suggests colitis, but
is nonspecific and may be secondary to underdistention.

MRI OF THE ABDOMEN WITH AND WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:

Visualized portions of the liver have homogeneous signal and enhancement. 
There is no intra or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  The gallbladder is
surgically absent.
There is atrophy of the pancreatic parenchyma.  The main pancreatic duct is
normal in caliber.  Pancreatic cystic lesions are seen throughout the
pancreas, the largest in the head measures 2.1 x 1.3 cm (05:18).
The kidneys and adrenals are normal.  Subcentimeter cortical renal cyst is
seen in the upper pole of the right kidney (14:28).  There is a single renal
artery present bilaterally.
The spleen is normal in size and signal.

MRI OF THE PELVIS WITH AND WITHOUT IV CONTRAST:

The bladder is normal.  The uterus and adnexa are normal.
There is no free fluid in the abdomen and pelvis.
There is no retroperitoneal, mesenteric or pelvic lymphadenopathy.
There is patchy hyper enhancement of the bone marrow in the sacrum
bilaterally, crossing the midline (13:64), in atypical appearance for a stress
fracture.  These area is not included in the imaging on T1 or STIR.  Dedicated
pelvic MRI is recommended to exclude infiltrative process.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  No evidence of inflammation throughout the small bowel.  Mild mucosal
hyper enhancement in the nondistended sigmoid colon suggests colitis, but is
nonspecific and may be secondary to underdistention.
2.  Patchy enhancement within the sacrum bilaterally, not fully characterized.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  Dedicated pelvic MRI is recommended to exclude
infiltrative process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been having nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for a few days now. It’s worse than before. I can’t keep anything down, not even water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any pain with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my belly pain is worse—around my belly button. It’s been chronic, but now it’s sharper. I also feel weak and kind of foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers, chills, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I’ve had chills and some shortness of breath, especially when I try to walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I see you were just here a few days ago. Your labs show your bicarbonate is low—down to 12. That means your body is a bit acidic, which can happen with severe vomiting or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds serious. Is that from the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be part of it. We also see your white blood cell count was high when you came in—13,000—but it’s coming down now. We’re checking for infections, including in your gut and urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on antibiotics before for gut issues. Could this be bacterial overgrowth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible, but your CT scan from the ER was normal—no blockages or inflammation. We did an MRI of your abdomen yesterday to look more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of inflammation in the small intestine. But there’s mild irritation in the sigmoid colon—could be colitis. We’re waiting on stool tests to see why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back. You have rotavirus—an intestinal virus. That explains the nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rotavirus? Isn’t that something kids get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but adults can get it too, especially those with weakened immune systems. Since you’re on prednisone and have GVHD, your body has a harder time fighting it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not from my gastroparesis or the nodules they saw last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rotavirus is the main cause now. Your chronic issues like gastroparesis and bacterial overgrowth may make symptoms worse, but this flare is viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can take a week or more to fully recover. We’re giving IV fluids and anti-nausea meds to help you feel better while your body fights the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your urine results. You have a UTI caused by Enterococcus. Because of your immune status, we’re treating it with nitrofurantoin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Bactrim for prevention. Why did I still get a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes bacteria become resistant or bypass the protection. Enterococcus can be tricky. Nitrofurantoin should work well based on the culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send you home with a prescription to finish the course. It’s important to complete it even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea seems better today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I sipped some broth without throwing up. But I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’re going to keep advancing your diet slowly. We also gave you IVIG yesterday for your immune support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I get that monthly. When’s my next dose due?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about a month. Your hematologist will coordinate that. We’ve also been managing your pain and nausea with IV meds, but we’re switching to oral ones as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI showed something else—we saw patchy bone signal in your sacrum. It’s not clear what it is. We recommend a pelvic MRI after discharge to check it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancer? My dad had cancer...

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not certain. It could be many things—some benign, some not. The pelvic MRI will give us a clearer picture. Your oncologist is aware and will help arrange it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ve sent a letter to your new primary care doctor too. You’re setting that up, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m switching to a new PCP in the city system. They already know I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve notified them about your hospitalization and the follow-up needs, including the MRI and your UTI treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is down to 5.5, and your bicarbonate is back to 24—normal. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. You’re tolerating food, your symptoms are controlled, and you’re walking around fine. We just need to make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been meaning to ask—should I restart my Miralax and stool softeners?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Since you still have some diarrhea from the virus, wait until your bowel movements normalize. Then you can restart them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with ondansetron—Zofran. Take it as needed for nausea, or before meals if eating is hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we ordered skull X-rays because of your headaches. The images are done, but radiology hasn’t read them yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely, since your neuro exam was normal. But we’ll send the results to your oncologist so they can review and follow up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’ve recovered well from the rotavirus infection and UTI treatment is set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea or diarrhea returns, or you develop fever, confusion, or trouble breathing, come back. Otherwise, follow up with your PCP and oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pelvic MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oncologist’s office will contact you to schedule it. It’s important to get it done to understand the bone finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same schedule—next dose in one month. They’ll call you to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed. Your husband can help you get ready to leave.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with worsening nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, following a recent hospitalization for similar symptoms. She has a complex history including chronic graft-versus-host disease, gastroparesis, and immunosuppression. Initial evaluation revealed metabolic acidosis and leukocytosis. Imaging showed no acute abdominal pathology but mild colitis on MRI. Stool testing confirmed rotavirus infection, explaining her gastroenteritis. She also had a complicated UTI with Enterococcus, treated with nitrofurantoin. During her stay, she received IV fluids, antiemetics, and supportive care, with gradual improvement. She tolerated oral intake, and symptoms resolved. A sacral bone marrow finding on MRI prompted a recommendation for outpatient pelvic MRI to rule out infiltrative disease. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans, including completing antibiotics, restarting bowel regimen when appropriate, and coordinating outpatient imaging and IVIG.
